candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: At the end of the year, the Profit and Loss Account of a partnership firm shows a credit balance (net profit). Which journal entry transfers this balance to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account?

options.text: Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c Dr. To Profit and Loss A/c
Profit and Loss A/c Dr. To Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c
Profit and Loss A/c Dr. To Interest on Capital A/c
Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c Dr. To Partners' Capital A/c

candidate.explanation: For a credit balance (net profit) the entry given is Profit and Loss A/c Dr. To Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c. Option A is the entry given for a debit balance (net loss), so it does not fit a net profit. Options C and D credit a different account, whereas the entry given for transferring the balance credits the Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c.

learning_objective.objective: Record the transfer of the Profit and Loss Account balance to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account.

candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: P and Q are partners who admit R with a guarantee that R's share of profit will not be less than Rs. 30,000. The guarantee is given by P and Q, who will bear any shortfall in the ratio 3:2. The firm's profit for the year is Rs. 1,50,000 and the profit sharing ratio of P, Q and R is 3:2:1. What amount of profit will P finally get?
candidate.explanation: R's share by the ratio is 1/6 of Rs. 1,50,000 = Rs. 25,000, which is Rs. 5,000 less than the guaranteed Rs. 30,000, so the shortfall is borne by the guaranteeing partners. P's share by the ratio is 3/6 of Rs. 1,50,000 = Rs. 75,000 and P bears 3/5 of Rs. 5,000 = Rs. 3,000, so P gets Rs. 72,000. Rs. 75,000 ignores the shortfall, Rs. 73,000 deducts 2/5 of Rs. 5,000 (Rs. 2,000), and Rs. 70,000 deducts the whole Rs. 5,000.

learning_objective.objective: Compute partners' shares of profit when a new partner is given a guarantee of minimum profit.

candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: A and B share profits in the ratio 2:1. C is admitted for 1/4 share of profits and brings in Rs. 20,000 as his capital. The remaining 3/4 share is divided between A and B in their old ratio 2:1. After all adjustments, the capitals of A and B are Rs. 45,000 and Rs. 15,000, and it is agreed that the capitals of the partners will be in proportion to their new profit shares, the total capital of the new firm being Rs. 80,000. What adjustment is needed in B's capital?
candidate.explanation: B's new share is 1/3 of the remaining 3/4, i.e. 1/4, so B's required capital is 1/4 of Rs. 80,000 = Rs. 20,000. B's capital is Rs. 15,000, which is Rs. 5,000 short, so B must bring in Rs. 5,000. Withdrawing Rs. 5,000 would apply to a surplus, which B does not have; Rs. 20,000 is the required capital, not the shortfall; and no adjustment is wrong because B's capital of Rs. 15,000 differs from Rs. 20,000.

learning_objective.objective: Adjust old partners' capitals to be proportionate to the new profit sharing ratio on admission of a partner.

candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: A firm has capital employed of Rs. 3,00,000 and the normal rate of return is 10%. Its average profit is Rs. 45,000. Using the capitalisation of super profit method, with Normal Profit = Capital Employed x Normal Rate/100 and Goodwill = Super Profit x 100/Normal Rate of Return, what is the value of goodwill?
candidate.explanation: Normal Profit = Rs. 3,00,000 x 10/100 = Rs. 30,000 and Super Profit = Rs. 45,000 - Rs. 30,000 = Rs. 15,000. Goodwill = Rs. 15,000 x 100/10 = Rs. 1,50,000. Rs. 15,000 is only the super profit, Rs. 4,50,000 is average profit x 100/10, and Rs. 30,000 is the normal profit; none of these is Super Profit x 100/10.

learning_objective.objective: Value goodwill by the capitalisation of super profit method.

candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: A company earned no profit in a year. Which statement about its obligations towards debentureholders is correct?

options.text: Interest on debentures is a charge on profits and is to be paid even if there is no profit
Interest on debentures is an appropriation of profits and need not be paid when there is no profit
Interest on debentures varies from year to year with the profits of the company
Interest on debentures is payable only if debentureholders exercise voting rights

candidate.explanation: The payment of interest is a charge on profits and is to be paid even if there is no profit. Option B is wrong because it is the payment of dividend that is an appropriation of profits. Option C is wrong because the rate of interest on debentures is prefixed, while the rate of return on shares may vary with profits. Option D is wrong because debentureholders do not normally enjoy voting rights and the payment of interest is not tied to them.

learning_objective.objective: Distinguish debentures from shares in respect of the nature of return.

items.defect_evidence: Recorded key is D, but the excerpt (F18) states that in dissolution of partnership the economic relationship between the partners continues in a changed form; option D says it comes to an end, which is the dissolution-of-firm column. The option the stem and excerpt actually establish is B (assets and liabilities are revalued and a new balance sheet is drawn). The explanation reaches D through the flawed step that the relationship ends in both cases.

candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: Two of the three partners of a firm agree by mutual consent to change the profit sharing ratio and continue the business. Which statement correctly describes what happens on this dissolution of partnership?

options.text: The business of the firm is closed and its books of account are closed
Assets and liabilities are revalued and a new balance sheet is drawn
The firm can be dissolved only by the court's order
The economic relationship between the partners comes to an end

candidate.explanation: Whenever a partnership is dissolved, the old agreement between the partners ends and so does their economic relationship. Option A and C describe the business being closed and court action, which do not apply to mutual agreement, and option B only describes a revaluation exercise. Hence D is correct.

learning_objective.objective: Differentiate between dissolution of partnership and dissolution of a partnership firm.

items.defect_evidence: Recorded key is A, but option D is also correct under F27: cash and cash equivalent is listed as current. Both A and D are fully defensible, so the item has two correct answers.

candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: Using the criteria for the current/non-current distinction in a company's balance sheet, which of the following is classified as current?

options.text: An asset expected to be realised within twelve months
An asset that is not involved in the operating cycle and is expected to be realised after more than twelve months
A liability that the entity has an unconditional right to defer settling for at least 12 months after the reporting period

candidate.explanation: An item is classified as current if it is expected to be realised or settled within twelve months. Hence an asset expected to be realised within twelve months is current. The other options are not correct.

learning_objective.objective: Classify balance sheet items as current or non-current.

items.defect_evidence: Key C (Rs. 800) is correct per F21 (share capital is debited with the amount called-up). The explanation's second sentence asserts that the balance of Share Forfeiture A/c must be transferred to General Reserve under the Companies Act; neither the stem nor F21/F22 says this (F22 shows the profit on reissue being transferred to Capital Reserve), so it is an unsupported and false rule.

candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: A company forfeits 100 shares of Rs. 10 each, issued at par, for non-payment of calls. Rs. 8 per share had been called up and Rs. 6 per share had been received. With what amount will Share Capital Account be debited on forfeiture?
candidate.explanation: On forfeiture, share capital account is debited with the amount called up on the shares forfeited, i.e. 100 x Rs. 8 = Rs. 800. The Rs. 600 received is not the amount debited, and Rs. 1,000 is the full face value although only Rs. 8 was called. The balance of Share Forfeiture A/c must always be transferred to General Reserve under the Companies Act after forfeiture, so no profit remains.

learning_objective.objective: Record the forfeiture of shares for non-payment of calls.

items.defect_evidence: The explanation states 96 / 12 = 6, which is an arithmetic error; 96 / 12 = 8 (option B). The recorded key A (6) is therefore wrong, even though the formula P/E = Market Price / EPS (F33) is applied correctly.

candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: The earnings per share of a company is Rs. 12 and the market price of its share is Rs. 96. Using P/E Ratio = Market Price of a share / Earnings per share, what is the price earning ratio?
candidate.explanation: P/E Ratio = Market Price of a share / Earnings per share = 96 / 12 = 6. The value 12 is only the EPS and 0.125 results from inverting the formula (12 / 96), so 6 is correct.

learning_objective.objective: Compute the price earning ratio from market price and earnings per share.
